questions.learningObjective: Interpret contrasting subsidence rates in ice-rich and silty permafrost

Thawing permafrost cools the soil because the ground loses its insulating snow

options.misconception: treats a measurement artefact as a physical difference

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why local sea level can rise without ocean volume changing
questions.stem: A coastal survey team's report must explain why measured sea level at a beach site can rise even when the ocean's volume is not changing.

answer.exemplar: Mean sea level at a site reflects the average level of the ocean surface plus the height of the land above it. If the crust subsides, or if the land rises isostatically as the ice above it melts, the same ocean surface sits at a higher elevation relative to the shore. Tides, storm surge and atmospheric pressure all shift the instantaneous reading as well, so a single visit can also show a higher reading without any change in ocean volume at all.

questions.explanation: Relative sea level depends on the height of the land as well as the ocean, so subsidence or glacial rebound can raise it locally. Attributing the rise to ocean volume alone ignores the land component.
questions.hint: Consider the land as well as the ocean.

options.misconception: ignores albedo when computing the effective temperature

options.text: About 300 kelvin, obtained by adding the reflected sunlight to the outgoing infrared
options.misconception: adds reflected shortwave into the infrared balance

options.text: About 215 kelvin, found by applying the albedo twice to the incoming flux

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement isolating the infrared response to carbon dioxide
questions.stem: A survey team must demonstrate that raising the carbon dioxide concentration produces a quantifiable change in outgoing infrared radiation. Describe an experiment that would isolate that response.

answer.exemplar: Use an atmospheric chamber containing air with a controlled carbon dioxide concentration, all other gases held fixed, and measure the outgoing infrared spectrum at the top of the chamber for several concentrations spanning the natural range. Radiate the chamber from below with a blackbody source so that surface temperature stays constant, which separates the direct effect of carbon dioxide on emission from any warming feedback. Regress the log of the measured infrared flux against the log concentration to obtain the forcing efficiency.

questions.explanation: Holding temperature fixed isolates the direct radiative effect of carbon dioxide, and the regression gives its efficiency. Warming the chamber would confound the direct effect with feedbacks.
questions.hint: Hold temperature fixed and vary only the gas.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why aerosol forcing differs between hemispheres
questions.stem: A survey team's report explains why the same aerosol event can cool one hemisphere and leave the other nearly unchanged.

answer.exemplar: Aerosol forcing is not spread evenly over the globe. Emissions from one hemisphere are concentrated over that hemisphere, so the reduction in incoming sunlight acts where the particles are and where clouds respond to them. The other hemisphere receives little of the extra aerosol, so its radiation budget changes little, and the temperature response in each hemisphere is also modulated by the circulation that redistributes heat between them. A single global figure for the forcing therefore hides a pattern with strongly regional consequences.

questions.explanation: Aerosol forcing is concentrated where the emissions are, so hemispheres respond differently. A single global average hides that spatial structure and its regional consequences.
questions.hint: Think about where the particles actually are.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of radiative equilibrium with the greenhouse effect removed
questions.stem: A survey team must test whether a planet's surface temperature stays at the radiative equilibrium value when the atmospheric greenhouse effect is switched off. Describe the experiment that would do this.

answer.exemplar: Run a coupled model in which the shortwave radiation scheme, surface and sea ice are kept exactly as in the reference run but the longwave greenhouse parameterisation is switched off, and then compare the resulting global mean surface temperature with the reference run. To confirm the result is radiative rather than dynamical, repeat the experiment with a fixed surface albedo and check that the outgoing infrared at the top of the atmosphere equals the absorbed solar flux in the adjusted run, which is the definition of radiative equilibrium.

questions.explanation: Removing only the longwave greenhouse term isolates its contribution, and checking the top-of-atmosphere balance confirms radiative equilibrium. Changing anything else confounds the test.
questions.hint: Change only the longwave treatment.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why specific humidity rises as air temperature rises
questions.stem: A survey team's briefing explains why the specific humidity of the air usually rises as the air temperature rises.

answer.exemplar: The amount of water vapour the air can hold before it becomes saturated is governed by the saturation vapour pressure, which increases exponentially with temperature through the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, rising by roughly seven percent for each degree Celsius of warming near typical surface temperatures. Because the actual mixing ratio changes much more slowly than the saturation value, a rise in temperature leaves the air further from saturation, so the specific humidity of the air, which is close to the mixing ratio, increases as the temperature rises.

questions.explanation: Saturation vapour pressure grows exponentially with temperature, so warming lets the air hold more vapour. Treating humidity as independent of temperature misses the Clausius-Clapeyron scaling.
questions.hint: Consider the Clausius-Clapeyron relation.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a chamber measurement of carbon release from thawing ground
questions.stem: A survey team must measure how much carbon a thawing permafrost site releases to the atmosphere. Describe the experimental design that would make that flux measurable.

answer.exemplar: Install a chamber over a set of paired plots, one with the surface soil kept frozen by insulation and one left to thaw naturally, and use a gas analyser to measure carbon dioxide concentration inside and outside the chamber over time. Compute the flux from the rate of change of concentration and the chamber volume, then scale it by the ground area under observation. Repeating the measurement across the full thaw season and across several sites of contrasting soil type gives a defensible seasonal and spatial estimate.

questions.explanation: Paired chambers with an insulated control separate the thaw effect from ordinary respiration, and the concentration slope gives the flux. Without the control, ordinary respiration is indistinguishable from thaw release.
questions.hint: Pair an insulated control with the thawed plot.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a change in overturning strength matters for regional climate
questions.stem: A survey team's briefing explains why a sustained decline in the overturning circulation would matter for regional climate even though the circulation carries no large heat reservoir.

answer.exemplar: The Atlantic overturning redistributes heat, salt and carbon between hemispheres and connects the surface with the deep ocean, so its strength governs how quickly heat and carbon are moved into the deep sea and how freshwater is carried around the basin. A weaker overturning therefore reduces the northern Atlantic's heat transport, changes the pathways of heat toward Europe, and alters the uptake of carbon by the deep ocean, all of which show up in regional climate and in sea level even though the overturning itself stores little energy.

questions.explanation: The overturning transports heat, salt and carbon and controls deep uptake, so its decline changes regional climate directly. Describing it as a heat store would miss its role as a conveyor.
questions.hint: Think about transport, not storage.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design an observational programme measuring ocean heat uptake
questions.stem: A survey team must determine how much heat the ocean has taken up over the past two decades. Describe the design of an observational programme that would deliver that estimate.

answer.exemplar: Combine repeat hydrographic sections along fixed transects with a network of moored and Argo profilers, and compute the change in heat content by differencing the two periods over the full ocean volume, correcting for the small area sampled by the moorings. Calibrate the instruments against a common reference and close the budget by comparing the ocean's estimated uptake with the residual left by the surface energy budget and the satellite estimate of the absorbed shortwave, so that a systematic error in any single component becomes visible.

questions.explanation: Repeat sections and float profiling over the full volume give the change in ocean heat content, and closing the budget exposes errors in any single component. One mooring covers too small a fraction of the ocean.
questions.hint: Combine full-depth sections with a float network.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why surface warming continues after carbon dioxide rises
questions.stem: A survey team's report explains why the increase in outgoing infrared that follows a rise in carbon dioxide does not stop the surface from warming.

answer.exemplar: Carbon dioxide is only one of the greenhouse gases in the system. When its concentration rises, the extra absorption of outgoing infrared reduces the energy lost to space at first, and the surface warms until the increased temperature restores the balance through the Stefan-Boltzmann relation. At the new equilibrium the outgoing infrared is again equal to the absorbed sunlight, but it equals it at a higher temperature. The radiative response of carbon dioxide alone therefore cannot explain the full size of the warming, which requires the feedbacks in the rest of the system.

questions.explanation: The surface warms until outgoing infrared again matches absorbed sunlight, so a higher temperature restores balance. Treating the extra infrared as the limit of warming ignores that equilibrium is restored warmer.
questions.hint: Ask what restores the energy balance.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a programme separating land motion from ocean volume
questions.stem: A survey team must separate the contributions of ocean volume, land motion and the starting position of the tide gauge to a local sea level record. Describe the design of the programme that would do this.

answer.exemplar: Run a continuous tide gauge with a datum tied to a stable benchmark, and in parallel measure vertical land motion at that site with a global navigation satellite system receiver and a co-located levelling survey. Combine the gauge's relative sea level record with an independent estimate of global mean sea level from satellite altimetry and from a global network of gauges corrected for land motion. The difference between the local record and the global component is the local contribution, while the datum survey removes the arbitrary offset in where the gauge was mounted.

questions.explanation: Correcting the gauge for land motion and removing the mounting offset separates local contributions from global ones. Without a datum survey, the constant part of the record is arbitrary.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why reducing aerosols can cause warming
questions.stem: A survey team's report explains why clearing aerosols from the atmosphere can raise global temperatures even though the particles themselves scatter sunlight.

answer.exemplar: Aerosols reflect sunlight directly, which cools the surface, but they also brighten clouds, and brighter clouds reflect more sunlight, which cools further. When aerosol pollution is reduced, both the direct cooling and the cloud brightening weaken at the same time, so the surface warms and clouds darken and let more sunlight through. The net effect of clearing aerosols is therefore warming, which is why aerosol reductions have been a source of additional warming while carbon dioxide reductions have been attempting to cool.

questions.explanation: Aerosols cool both directly and through brighter clouds, so reducing them warms the surface. Attribution that treats their net effect as warming wrongly assigns the change to carbon dioxide.
questions.hint: Consider both the direct and the cloud effect.

answer.exemplar: Use a chamber or optical bench in which the path length of carbon dioxide is increased in known steps while the total gas path and temperature are held fixed, and measure the change in outgoing infrared at each step. Because the additional carbon dioxide is added on top of a fixed background rather than replacing it, the incremental effect at each concentration is measured separately. Plotting the forcing against the logarithm of the concentration then shows whether each doubling adds a similar increment, which is the signature of logarithmic behaviour.

questions.explanation: Adding carbon dioxide in known steps and measuring each increment tests whether the effect grows in the way a logarithm requires. A single comparison of two concentrations cannot establish that.
questions.hint: Add the gas in known incremental steps.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a fast global rise can coexist with little local change
questions.stem: A survey team's briefing explains why a region with the fastest rise in global mean sea level may still show little local change at the coast.

answer.exemplar: Global mean sea level is only an average, and the local response depends on how the ocean's volume change is distributed, on how the solid Earth moves vertically in response to the melting ice, and on how the ocean's surface tilts as the gravitational attraction of the shrinking ice sheet is removed. Near a large melting ice sheet the surface can tilt away from it and the crust can subside or rebound, and these regional effects can dominate the small global signal. A locally tidally dominated or subsiding coast can therefore show little or even opposite change.

questions.explanation: Regional ocean dynamics and vertical land motion can dominate the global mean signal at a given coast. Reading the global figure as the local one overlooks those regional contributions.
questions.hint: Consider regional adjustments to the mean.

answer.exemplar: Use more than one observing method so that an error in one system cannot produce the whole signal: a deep array of moorings with current meters and temperature and salinity sensors, a fleet of autonomous floats profiling to the sea floor, and a hydrographic section repeated along the same line in different seasons. questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish effective radiating temperature from surface temperature
questions.stem: A survey team's briefing explains why a planet's surface temperature can be warmer than its effective radiating temperature.

answer.exemplar: The effective radiating temperature is the temperature the planet would have if it emitted as a perfect blackbody with no atmosphere and absorbed the same sunlight. A real surface is usually warmer than that value because the atmosphere returns part of the infrared that the surface emits, so the surface does not have to supply the whole outgoing flux itself. The effective radiating temperature therefore describes the planet's energy budget in a simplified way, while the surface temperature reflects the additional greenhouse warming above it.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse return of surface infrared warms the surface above the blackbody equivalent of its absorbed energy. Equating the two temperatures ignores the atmosphere's return of radiation.
questions.hint: Ask what the atmosphere returns to the surface.

questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment demonstrating the Clausius-Clapeyron behaviour
questions.stem: A survey team must show that the moisture holding capacity of air rises faster than linearly with temperature. Describe the experiment that would demonstrate this.

answer.exemplar: Prepare a set of saturated samples at temperatures spanning a range, from cool to warm, and measure the actual vapour pressure over each saturated sample with a chilled dew point hygrometer while the temperature is held steady. Tabulate the measured saturation vapour pressure against temperature and then plot the logarithm of the vapour pressure against the reciprocal of the absolute temperature. A straight line on that plot demonstrates the Clausius-Clapeyron behaviour, and the curvature of the vapour pressure against temperature shows that the growth is exponential rather than linear.

questions.explanation: Measuring saturation vapour pressure across temperatures and plotting the logarithm against reciprocal temperature tests the Clausius-Clapeyron prediction. A linear increase in capacity would not produce that straight line.
questions.hint: Plot the logarithm against reciprocal temperature.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why permafrost carbon release is a feedback rather than a forcing
questions.stem: A survey team's briefing explains why the carbon released by thawing permafrost is described as a feedback rather than an initial forcing.

answer.exemplar: A forcing is a change imposed on the climate system from outside it, such as a change in solar output or in greenhouse gas concentration. Thawing is not imposed: it is a response to warming, which then releases carbon dioxide and methane that produce further warming. Because the process amplifies a change that has already occurred rather than causing it, it is classified as a feedback, and its strength is measured by how much extra warming results per kelvin of initial warming.

questions.explanation: Thawing is a response to warming that then causes more warming, so it is a feedback rather than an imposed forcing. Classifying it as a forcing would reverse the direction of causation.
questions.hint: Ask whether the process drives or amplifies warming.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why ocean heat uptake efficiency changes as the climate warms
questions.stem: A survey team's briefing explains why the ocean's heat uptake efficiency is expected to change as the climate warms.

answer.exemplar: The ocean takes up heat only while the sea surface is warmer than the atmosphere above it, so the uptake depends on the temperature difference across the air-sea interface and on the efficiency of the turbulent exchange. As the atmosphere warms, that difference shrinks and the mixing that carries heat downwards becomes weaker, while the increasing stratification of the upper ocean makes it harder for heat to reach the depths where it can be stored effectively. The ocean therefore takes up a smaller share of the excess energy as the system warms, which is one of the reasons the surface warms faster than the deep ocean.

questions.explanation: A shrinking air-sea temperature difference and stronger stratification reduce the ocean's ability to take up and store heat. Assuming constant efficiency would ignore these changes.
questions.hint: Think about the air-sea difference and stratification.

answer.exemplar: Install a continuous tide gauge to measure relative sea level and a dual-frequency satellite receiver on a stable benchmark nearby to measure vertical land motion at the same site, so that the two contributions can be separated. Combine these with satellite altimetry and a global gauge network to establish the global component over the same period, and compare the site's residual against regional subsidence maps compiled from groundwater extraction records. If the residual tracks the subsidence field rather than the global curve, the local contribution is land motion.

questions.explanation: Separating relative sea level into a global and a land-motion part requires both a tide gauge and a co-located vertical land motion measurement. Reading the record without that split cannot attribute the rise.
questions.hint: Measure both the water and the land.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change in surface water density after a melt season
questions.stem: A survey team's table lists the density of surface water in the subpolar North Atlantic before and after a strong melt season, showing a fall from 27.6 to 27.2 kilograms per cubic metre. What does the change indicate?

options.text: The fresher water is now less dense, so it is less likely to sink and drive the overturning
The denser water will now sink more readily and strengthen the overturning circulation
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the density change

options.text: The water has warmed by 0.4 degrees Celsius, which fully explains the change
options.misconception: converts a density change directly into a temperature change

options.text: The surface layer has become saltier, since salt and density always move together
options.misconception: confuses density with salinity in freshened water

questions.explanation: Freshening lowers density, so the surface water becomes less likely to sink and the overturning weakens. The density change does not correspond to the temperature change suggested, and freshened water is less salty.
questions.hint: Relate density to salinity and sinking.
